intro: A network needs addresses: without them, no machine can find another. Here you can work out subnets, send a ping, follow a DNS query across the internet and look up which service listens on which port.

subnet.explain: An IPv4 address has 32 bits. The mask splits them: the leading bits name the network, the rest the machine in it. Machines with the same network part reach each other directly - everyone else only through a gateway.
subnet.summary: Prefix /{prefix, number}: {hosts, plural, one {# usable address} other {# usable addresses}} in this network.

errors.invalidAddress: That is not a valid IPv4 address: four numbers from 0 to 255, separated by dots.
errors.invalidPrefix: The prefix runs from /0 to /32 - or write a mask such as 255.255.255.0.
errors.invalidMask: This mask is not contiguous: all the ones must come first, then all the zeros.

subnet.bitsLabel: The address's 32 bits: {network, number} bits for the network, {host, number} bits for the machine.
subnet.legendNetwork: {count, plural, one {# network bit} other {# network bits}}
subnet.legendHost: {count, plural, one {# host bit} other {# host bits}}

unspecified.name: Unspecified
unspecified.note: 0.0.0.0/8 means "this network" or "no address yet" - a machine asking DHCP at start-up sends from 0.0.0.0.

loopback.name: Loopback
loopback.note: 127.0.0.0/8 never leaves the machine: whoever talks to 127.0.0.1 talks to itself.

private.name: Private (RFC 1918)
private.note: Private addresses only count inside your own network. They reach the internet through NAT: the router swaps them for its one public address.

sharedCgnat.name: Carrier-grade NAT
sharedCgnat.note: 100.64.0.0/10 is handed out by providers who have too few public addresses themselves - a NAT behind the NAT.

linkLocal.name: Link-local (APIPA)
linkLocal.note: A machine gives itself an address from 169.254.0.0/16 when no DHCP server answers. Windows 98 called it APIPA - and it usually meant: check the cable.

documentation.name: Documentation
documentation.note: These ranges (RFC 5737) are reserved for examples and never routed on the internet - which is why this site uses them for its simulations.

multicast.name: Multicast
multicast.note: 224.0.0.0/4 addresses a group rather than one machine: whoever joins receives the packets.

reserved.name: Reserved
reserved.note: 240.0.0.0/4 has been reserved for later since the eighties - and is still unused.

broadcast.name: Limited broadcast
broadcast.note: 255.255.255.255 reaches every machine on the local network, but never a router beyond it.

public.name: Public
public.note: A public address is unique worldwide and reachable on the internet - unless a firewall stands in front of it.

roles.network: This is the network address itself: it names the whole network and belongs to no machine.
roles.broadcast: This is the broadcast address: a packet sent to it goes to everyone on the network - no machine may use it.

subnet.pointToPoint: /31 is a point-to-point link between two routers (RFC 3021): no network or broadcast address, both addresses are usable.
subnet.singleHost: /32 names exactly one address - that is how single machines appear in routing tables and firewall rules.

gateway.title: Does the gateway fit?
gateway.explain: Exactly the question the 1995 puzzle asked: a machine sends everything outside its network to its gateway - and it must be able to reach it directly.
gateway.label: Default gateway
gateway.invalid: Enter a valid IPv4 address for the gateway.

verdicts.ok: The gateway is in the same network and is a host address. That is the way out.
verdicts.otherSubnet: The gateway is in another network. The machine cannot reach it directly - and so nothing outside its network.
verdicts.isNetwork: That is the network address. A gateway needs a real host address.
verdicts.isBroadcast: That is the broadcast address. A gateway needs a real host address.
verdicts.isSelf: That is the machine's own address. It cannot be its own gateway.

split.title: Split the network
split.explain: Every extra bit in the prefix halves the network. That is how a company divides one network into floors, departments or VLANs.
split.label: Into how many parts?
split.more: … and {count, plural, one {# more} other {# more}}

subnet.truth: This is the one truth of 1995: a network needs addresses. The mask decides who is a neighbour - and who can only be reached through the gateway.

ping.simulation: Simulation: a browser may not send a real ping, and this page sends nothing onto the network. The targets and times come from the same prepared routes as the Traceroute app - times that light in glass fibre really needs.
ping.explain: ping sends a small ICMP packet (an "echo request") and waits for the echo. The time in between is the round trip - there and back. This is how it looked under Windows 95.

notes.route: All four packets came back. The TTL dropped by one per router on the way - {hops, plural, one {# stop} other {# stops}} to the target.
notes.loopback: There's no place like 127.0.0.1: the packet never left the machine, which is why it takes less than a millisecond.
notes.silent: No answer. This address is reserved for examples - and many real machines ignore ping too, because a firewall drops ICMP. Silence does not mean nobody is there.
notes.unknown: The simulation does not know this name. For real, a DNS query would have come before the first packet - try it in the DNS tab.

ping.ttl: TTL means "time to live": each router takes one off, and at zero the packet is dropped. That way no packet circles forever - and that is exactly what traceroute exploits.

dns.simulation: Simulation: the query runs over a prepared zone of names under .example, which are reserved for examples. Nothing leaves this browser.
dns.explain: People remember names, machines need addresses. DNS translates - one step at a time: the resolver asks the root servers, they point to the top-level domain, that points to the responsible name server, and only that one knows the answer.

types.A: A - the IPv4 address for the name.
types.AAAA: AAAA - the IPv6 address for the name.
types.MX: MX - which server accepts e-mail for this domain; the lower number is tried first.
types.TXT: TXT - free text, today mostly for e-mail rules (SPF) and verification.
types.CNAME: CNAME - an alias: this name is only another name for another name.

notes.cached: This time the answer came from the cache: 0 ms instead of a trip around the world. That is what the TTL is for - how long a resolver may keep the answer.
notes.found: Found. The resolver keeps this answer for {ttl, plural, one {# second} other {# seconds}} - ask again right away.
notes.nxdomain: NXDOMAIN: this name does not exist. Even a "no" is kept for a while, by the way.
notes.cname: The name was an alias (CNAME); the resolver followed it to the address.
notes.hello: If you read TXT records for fun, you are in the right place.

ports.explain: An address finds the machine, a port the program on it. There are 65,536 ports per protocol; a service listens on a fixed one - a web server on 443.

ranges.wellKnown: Well-known port (0-1023): for standard services, once openable only with administrator rights.
ranges.registered: Registered port (1024-49151): recorded with IANA for particular programs.
ranges.dynamic: Dynamic port (49152-65535): your machine picks these itself, as the sender of a connection.

ports.invalid: Ports run from 0 to 65535; services are searched with letters.
ports.noMatch: No service in this list matches.

stories.elite: 31337 - "eleet" in hacker spelling, meaning "elite". In the late nineties the remote-control trojan Back Orifice listened here; whoever found the port open knew what was going on.

ports.caption: Common ports with protocol, service name and use

services.ssh: SSH: encrypted remote login - every administrator's tool
services.telnet: Telnet: remote login in plain text, today only in the lab
services.smtp: SMTP: servers passing e-mail between each other
services.dhcpServer: DHCP, server side: hands out addresses
services.dhcpClient: DHCP, client side: asks for an address
services.imap: IMAP: reading e-mail on the server
services.snmp: SNMP: monitoring devices on the network
services.ldap: LDAP: directory services such as Active Directory
services.https: HTTPS: the web over TLS - this site too
services.syslog: Syslog: log messages to a central server
services.submission: SMTP submission: your mail program handing in e-mail
services.httpAlt: HTTP, alternative: often test servers and proxies

ports.firewall: Which ports may be open is the firewall's decision - the puzzle of the last era.
ports.firewallLink: To the firewall in the journey
